opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's useful to separate them by *when* the computation happens and *where* the knowledge ends up living.

Model-free RL is fundamentally about amortization. You interact with the environment a lot, you collect experience, and you slowly distill what you've learned into the weights of a network, either a policy that maps states directly to actions, or a value function that tells you how good a state or action is. At test time you just do a forward pass. There's no deliberation. All the "thinking" happened during training, spread across millions of trajectories, and the network has compressed it into something like an intuition. The problem it's solving is credit assignment: I did a bunch of things and got a reward much later, so which of those actions actually mattered? Temporal-difference learning, policy gradients, all of that machinery is about propagating that sparse signal back to the decisions that caused it.

Monte Carlo tree search does something different. It's decision-time computation. You're in a specific state, and you spend compute right now, looking ahead, simulating "if I do this, then they do that," expanding the tree, backing up values, and focusing your search budget on the branches that look promising. It needs a model of the environment, whether that's the actual game rules like in Go or chess, or a learned dynamics model like in MuZero. And it gives you a much better answer for this particular state than your raw intuition would, because you're spending more compute on it.

The interesting part is how they fit together, which is really the AlphaGo and AlphaZero insight. MCTS is a policy improvement operator. Take your network's policy, run search on top of it, and the visit counts coming out of the search form a better policy than what you started with. Then you train the network to imitate that improved policy, so the network gets sharper, so the next search starts from a better prior, and you get this bootstrapping loop. Search makes the fast system smarter, and the fast system makes search more efficient by pruning the tree to moves worth considering.

So the cleanest way I'd put it is that model-free RL is learning System 1, a fast, amortized intuition, and MCTS is a form of System 2, explicit, expensive, local deliberation. The most powerful systems use the slow one to generate training targets for the fast one.

That's also why I think it's such a relevant frame right now with language models. A lot of what people call reasoning or test-time compute is asking the same question: how much do you bake into the weights versus how much do you figure out on the fly? And can you take what you figured out on the fly and feed it back into training? It's the same structure, just in a much messier, open-ended action space where you don't have clean game rules to search over.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the cleanest way to think about it is that they're attacking the same problem from opposite directions. Both of them are trying to answer the question: given the state I'm in right now, what's the best thing to do? But they differ in where the compute gets spent.

Model-free RL is trying to amortize that answer. You go out, you collect a ton of experience, you see which actions led to good outcomes, and you compress all of that into a policy or a value function. So at test time you've already done the hard work. You look at the state, you do one forward pass, and the network just tells you what to do. All the "thinking" happened during training, and what you're left with is basically a reflex. It's cheap at inference, but it's only as good as the data you trained on, and if you drop it in a situation that's a little off-distribution, it has no way to recover. It can't reason its way out of a situation it hasn't seen.

Monte Carlo tree search is the opposite bet. It says, I'm not going to pre-compute the answer, I'm going to spend compute at decision time. You have a model of the world, a simulator or a learned dynamics model, and you literally roll out futures. You try action A, you see where that leads, you try action B, you expand the promising branches, and you back up those values to figure out what to do right now. So it's doing search, it's deliberative, and the key property is that the more compute you give it, the better the decision gets. You can't say that about a fixed policy network.

The thing that made AlphaGo and AlphaZero so interesting is that they didn't pick one, they married them. The policy and value networks are the model-free part, they're the amortized intuition that tells the search where to look so it doesn't have to expand a hundred million nodes. And then the tree search is the slow, deliberate part that corrects the intuition when the intuition is wrong. Then you close the loop: the search produces better targets than the raw network would have, you distill those back into the network, and the intuition gets better. It's a kind of System 1, System 2 thing, if you want to use the Kahneman framing.

Where this gets really hard, and this is what I care about in robotics, is that MCTS kind of presupposes you have a model you can trust to roll forward. In Go the rules are the model, it's perfect. In the real world, if your learned dynamics model is slightly wrong, the search will happily exploit those errors and find plans that look amazing in simulation and fall apart the second you execute them. So in practice, model-free methods have been the workhorse for a lot of real-world stuff precisely because they sidestep the problem of having to model the world accurately. But I think the long-term answer looks a lot more like AlphaZero than like pure model-free. You want the amortized policy for speed and the search for robustness, and you want the model to be good enough that searching over it actually helps instead of hurts.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as a distinction between doing the computation at training time and doing it at decision time. With Monte Carlo tree search, you’re at a particular state, and you explore possible futures: if I take this action, and then this happens, what outcome do I get? You use those simulated trajectories to decide what to do now.

With model-free reinforcement learning, you learn a policy or a value function from experience. You’re trying to capture enough of what worked in the past that, when you encounter a new state, you can make a good decision without explicitly searching through those futures. In that sense, you’re amortizing the cost of figuring out how to act across many decisions.

And they’re complementary. A learned policy can tell your search which branches are promising, and a learned value function can evaluate positions without having to simulate all the way to the end. Then the results of search can become training targets for the policy. So search spends additional computation on a particular problem, while learning lets you carry some of the benefit of that computation into future problems.

sol-6.1.text:
The distinction I’d make is between learning how to act and searching for how to act. In model-free reinforcement learning, you interact with an environment and use the rewards you get to train a policy or a value function. Eventually, you want that policy to produce a good action without having to explicitly think through all the possible futures.

With Monte Carlo tree search, you have some way of simulating what happens next. You can try an action, explore possible continuations, and use those simulated outcomes to decide what to do right now. You’re spending computation at decision time rather than putting all of it into training.

And those are complementary. You can learn a policy that tells the search which branches are promising, and a value function that tells it whether a position is good without having to simulate all the way to the end. Then you can train the policy on the better decisions that search produces. So search can improve the policy, and the policy can make search more efficient.
